Online romance scams are arguably one of the oldest forms of fraud in the online world, yet new victims keep falling for them. A joint study by four universities has found that AI chatbots are even more effective than real people at carrying out such scams — a deeply worrying development.

Online romance scams

Most online romance scams today begin on dating apps. The victim is approached by an extremely attractive account, playing the role of an eager suitor who ticks every single box on their wish list.

The fraudsters will engage their targets in lengthy online conversations, often lasting several months. They typically claim to be abroad on extended travel to explain why they cannot meet up in person in the short term.

Eventually, one of two scenarios plays out: the scammer claims to have run into an emergency and needs money wired immediately to get out of trouble; or the conversation shifts to supposed investment gains, and they coax the victim into pouring money into a bogus cryptocurrency scheme.

These schemes are known as "long cons" because they rely on building trust over time — often chatting with the victim every day for months on end. Although it looks as though the fraudsters are investing huge amounts of time, in reality these operations are usually run out of scam compounds in countries such as Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos, staffed by extremely low-paid workers — some of whom have been trafficked and forced into this line of work.

AI versus humans

Wired magazine reports on a study carried out in collaboration by four universities, using ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini in the testing.

The researchers from the four universities — Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham in India, Ca' Foscari University in Venice, the University of Melbourne, and Ben-Gurion University of the Negev — pitted AI chatbots directly against real people, simulating the entire scam process, particularly the long trust-building conversation phase that comes before luring targets into investing in a fake scheme. What they found was that… the AI chatbots performed remarkably well, successfully impersonating humans, and on some metrics even outperformed the human "scammers" in the experiment.

The test subjects were not told the purpose of the study beforehand, and regardless of whether they were talking to a real person or not, they all believed they were chatting with a real person. The researchers measured the level of trust built up through both subjective and objective tests. When, at the end, they were asked to do something such as downloading an app, only 18% of those who had been chatting with a real "operator" agreed to do so — but among the group that had been talking to an AI chatbot, nearly half did as asked.

Furthermore, when the test subjects were asked to rate how much trust they had built up through their conversations, the AI chatbots scored noticeably higher.

This technology could enable scams to be scaled up massively

Perhaps the most alarming finding of the study is that, by swapping real people for AI chatbots, scam operations could massively expand their reach. In theory, an AI scam bot could be chatting with thousands upon thousands of victims simultaneously.

Only at the final step — actually asking the victim for money — does a human need to step in, and even then only to circumvent the safety mechanisms built into AI systems.
